misconceptions.description: Treating a prompt log as a raw chat transcript to keep, rather than as curated evidence of design decisions and why prompts changed
misconceptions.trigger: learner pastes the full unannotated chat history as the log
misconceptions.feedback: A prompt log is evidence, not a transcript. For each kept prompt, record what you were trying to fix and what the output changed.

misconceptions.description: Logging only the final successful prompt and deleting the failed attempts, hiding the reasoning that justified the final choice
misconceptions.trigger: learner keeps only the prompt that worked
misconceptions.feedback: Rejected prompts are part of the evidence. Keep at least one failed attempt and say why it was rejected; that is the design judgment.

misconceptions.description: Assuming that having a long prompt log proves the design is rigorous, regardless of whether the log connects to learning decisions
misconceptions.trigger: learner points to log length as evidence of effort
misconceptions.feedback: Length is not rigor. The log earns credit only where a prompt change is tied to a learning goal or constraint, not effort alone.

misconceptions.description: Recording prompt edits without noting how each edit changed the artifact or whether it improved the learning function
misconceptions.trigger: log lists prompt versions but never states the effect of each change
misconceptions.feedback: Tie each prompt revision to an observed change in the output and to whether it served the learning goal. Edits without effects are noise.
